title: 3D printed thermal cloak hides objects from infrared cameras
excerpt: A hybrid aluminum-rubber lattice guides heat around objects, making them invisible to thermal imaging while staying protected from extreme temperatures.
body:
A 3-D-printed aluminum lattice filled with a rubber-like polymer can steer heat around a hidden object, so an infrared camera sees no temperature disturbance. The device keeps the interior at a constant temperature while the surrounding thermal field remains unchanged, even when heat arrives from many directions. The experiment shows that a fully three-dimensional thermal cloak is no longer a theoretical curiosity.

The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign team, professor Shelly Zhang, postdoctoral researcher Weichen Li, graduate student Yibo Wang, and collaborator Ole Sigmund of the Technical University of Denmark, built and tested the cloak, publishing the results in *Nature Communications*. Their work moves thermal cloaking from flat, single-direction demonstrations to a practical system that can protect complex shapes in real-world environments.  

Readers will learn how the hybrid lattice is fabricated, how transformation thermotics guides its design, and what the infrared tests revealed about direction-independent performance.

## Hybrid aluminum-rubber lattice redirects heat

The cloak consists of an aluminum scaffold produced by 3-D metal printing. Thin struts form a three-dimensional network that provides high-conductivity pathways. After printing, the empty spaces are cast with a rubber-like polymer that conducts heat poorly. This combination yields a composite whose effective thermal conductivity can be tuned independently along each axis.

Because aluminum conducts heat quickly, it channels thermal energy along the lattice. The surrounding polymer slows transfer in the gaps, forcing the flow to follow the intended routes. The result is a guided heat stream that skirts the concealed volume, much like water flowing around a stone. The interior stays insulated, while the exterior temperature gradient appears as if the object were not present.

## Transformation thermotics supplies the design recipe

Transformation thermotics treats heat flow as a coordinate transformation. By mapping a region of space to a new set of thermal properties, one can dictate how heat should bend around that region. Earlier experiments applied this idea only to flat surfaces or to heat moving in a single direction, limiting them to two dimensions.

The researchers asked what material structure could provide the full range of anisotropic conductivities needed for a perfect three-dimensional cloak. Their answer was a lattice whose geometry can be adjusted separately along three orthogonal directions. This flexibility expands the achievable conductivity spectrum far beyond prior designs, approaching the ideal values predicted by the theory. The study demonstrates that the abstract mathematics of transformation thermotics can be realized with a printable, hybrid material system.

## Infrared camera tests prove direction-independent cloaking

To evaluate performance, the team placed the cloak between a hot plate and a cold sink, creating a temperature difference that drove heat through the surrounding space. An infrared camera recorded the surface temperature pattern while a test object sat inside the lattice.

The images showed a continuous temperature field across the cloak, with no visible disturbance where the object was located. Tests were repeated with heat approaching from multiple angles; each time the infrared camera displayed the same uninterrupted pattern, confirming that the cloak works regardless of heat direction.  

At the same time, the interior temperature remained stable, demonstrating that the device not only hides the thermal signature but also protects the concealed item from extreme temperatures.

## Potential applications and next steps

The ability to hide complex shapes from thermal imaging while maintaining internal temperature stability opens several avenues:

* Cooling of microchips where hot spots must be masked from external sensors.  
* Protection of delicate electronics that operate in harsh thermal environments.  
* Stealth technology that reduces the thermal footprint of equipment.  

Future work will likely focus on scaling the lattice to larger objects, optimizing the polymer fill for durability, and integrating the cloak into existing thermal management systems.

## The takeaway

A 3-D-printed aluminum-rubber lattice can guide heat around an object, making it invisible to infrared cameras from any direction while keeping the interior temperature stable. The key is a geometry that provides independently tunable conductivities, turning transformation-thermodics theory into a practical, printable material system.
